question: A service function decorated with @transaction.atomic saves an uploaded file to object storage, then creates the related DB rows; row creation raises. What must the except block do, and why?
choices: Nothing — atomic() rolls back the whole operation, including the stored file
Re-raise inside a nested atomic() block so a savepoint also covers the file write
Delete the stored blob explicitly before re-raising: storage writes are never enrolled in the DB transaction, so rollback alone leaves an orphaned file
Call save(update_fields=[]) on the document so no partially-written rows persist
explanation: transaction.atomic rolls back rows, not side effects: a blob written to disk or object storage sits outside the database transaction, so on exception the rows vanish but the file survives as an orphan. The seam must track what it wrote and clean up itself — doc.file.delete(save=False), then re-raise so the DB rollback still happens. Nested atomic() blocks only add savepoints over DB state, and update_fields shapes a future write rather than undoing anything. This is also why validating everything before the first write is so valuable: a rejection then needs no cleanup at all.

question: A DocumentAttachment table uses a GenericForeignKey — a content_type FK plus a plain object_id column — so one table can attach documents to any model with no schema change per new target. What integrity cost does this design accept, and where must it be repaid?
choices: object_id carries no database FK constraint, so deleting a target row leaves attachment rows dangling; the DB cannot cascade, and cleanup must be reimplemented in application code — e.g. a pre_delete receiver wired for every allowed target model
ContentType rows must be created by hand for each new model, so a forgotten row makes attachments to that model fail at runtime
Every new attachable model requires a migration to widen object_id to the new model's primary-key type
limit_choices_to on the content_type FK is enforced by the database on every insert, so the cost is write throughput rather than integrity
explanation: A GFK trades referential integrity for schema flexibility: because object_id is a plain value column, the database has no idea the link exists — no cascade, no PROTECT, no orphan prevention. That guarantee doesn't disappear; it moves into code. And since deletes arrive from many paths (instance deletes, queryset deletes, FK cascades, admin actions), the robust repayment is a pre_delete signal receiver registered for every model in the attachment registry — a property of the models themselves rather than of each delete path. The distractors invert the design's facts: Django auto-creates ContentType rows at migrate time, object_id keeps one fixed type precisely so new targets need no migration, and limit_choices_to is evaluated only in forms and the admin — it enforces nothing at the database or API layer.

question: A pre_delete receiver on Order detaches its DocumentAttachments; it is wired in AppConfig.ready() and works from the admin, the shell, and API deletes. A cleanup data migration then deletes obsolete orders via apps.get_model('store', 'Order') inside RunPython — and staging ends up with dangling attachment rows: the receiver never fired. Why?
choices: AppConfig.ready() doesn't run for manage.py migrate — only for request-serving processes — so no receiver was connected during the migration run; moving the connect calls to the top of models.py fixes it
Queryset .delete() takes a bulk fast path that skips per-instance signals; the migration should loop and call instance.delete() one row at a time so each fires pre_delete
Signals are deferred until transaction commit, and each migration runs inside its own transaction that the migrate process finalizes after dispatch has already been torn down

Signals dispatch by sender identity, and RunPython never hands you your classes: the apps argument resolves models against the historical snapshot registry — plain reconstructed classes pinned to that migration's point in schema history, distinct objects from the live classes your receiver is connected to. A delete through the snapshot Order is a delete from a different sender, so the wiring never matches; by design, since a migration must stay runnable years later when today's code no longer resembles that snapshot. The honest patterns: make the migration self-contained (delete the attachment rows explicitly in the same RunPython), or do the cleanup operationally through a management command, which uses live classes — service seam, signals, and all
explanation: The mechanism is two Django facts composing: receivers registered with a sender are keyed to a specific class object, and RunPython's apps registry deliberately does not contain your class objects — it rebuilds bare model classes from the migration graph's recorded state, so the code runs against the schema as it was, independent of what models.py says today. That independence is the entire reliability contract of data migrations (they must apply cleanly on a fresh database long after the code has moved on), and its price is that everything attached to your live classes — custom methods, managers' overrides, and signal wiring — is absent. The dangling rows follow directly: the snapshot Order deletes fine, but the sender your receiver listens for was never involved. The right responses respect the boundary rather than fight it: a migration should carry its own cleanup logic inline (idempotent, snapshot-only), or the operation belongs in a management command where live classes — and therefore the single seam and the registry-driven signals — apply. The distractors invent plausible machinery: ready() runs whenever the app registry initializes, management commands included — and module-top wiring is the AppRegistryNotReady trap ready() exists to prevent; queryset deletes are covered — the deletion Collector fetches rows and fires pre_delete for each before the bulk DELETE, which is exactly why admin and shell deletes worked; and lifecycle signals fire inline at delete time — deferral-to-commit describes transaction.on_commit, a separate opt-in hook, not the signal framework.

question: A backfill management command attaches 5,000 legacy invoice PDFs to their Orders through the document service. For safety, the author decorates the whole handle() with @transaction.atomic. Item 4,993 raises on a corrupt PDF: three hours of writes roll back, and the re-run must redo everything. Where should the transaction boundary sit, and why?
choices: Keep the whole-run transaction but wrap each item in try/except and continue on failure — the outer atomic still guarantees the batch is consistent, while the per-item catch stops one corrupt file from aborting the loop

Remove the transaction entirely: the sheet's own gotcha says atomic() never rolls back the stored file bytes anyway, so wrapping a file-writing batch in a transaction is safety theatre — better to run bare and rely on the idempotent re-run to converge

The boundary must match the unit of work, and each PDF is an independent unit: open one atomic() per iteration. Each item's rows — the Document and its attachment — commit or roll back together; a corrupt PDF is logged and skipped without touching its 4,992 successful peers; and progress commits incrementally, so a crash resumes instead of restarting. Paired with the command's idempotency check (skip orders already carrying their PDF), the re-run flies past completed work. The whole-run transaction answered a question nobody asked — 'all 5,000 or none' — and charged for it twice: hours of lost work on any failure, and a three-hour transaction holding row locks against the live database the entire time. The granularity rule generalizes: per-request atomicity for user actions, per-iteration atomicity for batch loops

Keep the outer atomic and nest an inner atomic() per item: inner blocks become savepoints, so a failing item rolls back alone while the outer transaction preserves the all-or-nothing guarantee for the batch as a whole
explanation: Transaction scope is a design decision about what must succeed or fail together, and the author's mistake was defaulting to 'everything' without asking whether the items are coupled. They aren't: order 17's PDF attaching successfully is not invalidated by order 4,993's corruption, so binding them into one atomic unit manufactures a coupling that only ever costs — lost work on failure, a giant transaction holding locks and pinning the database's cleanup machinery for hours, and nothing gained, because no invariant spans two different orders' documents. Per-iteration atomic() aligns the boundary with the real invariant (a Document row must never exist without its attachment rows — that pair is the unit) and buys the operational properties a batch needs: skip-and-continue on bad items, incremental commit so a crash resumes, and synergy with the idempotency check that makes re-runs cheap. The distractors each preserve the oversized transaction while patching one symptom. Catch-and-continue inside a single transaction has a hard failure mode on PostgreSQL: after any errored SQL statement the connection refuses further statements ('current transaction is aborted') until rollback, so the loop's remaining items fail regardless — and even when the exception fires before any SQL, the crash-loses-all and lock-duration costs stand. Dropping transactions misreads the blob gotcha: the file bytes being outside the transaction is an argument for the service's compensating delete, not against row atomicity — bare execution can leave a Document row committed without its attachments, exactly the partial state atomic() exists to prevent. And nested atomics do isolate a failing item via savepoints — that half is true — but savepoints fix error isolation, not commit granularity: nothing commits until the outer block exits, so the three-hour lock window and the crash-at-4,999-loses-everything property survive intact.

question: All API error observability runs through a custom DRF EXCEPTION_HANDLER. Serializer validation failures log fine, but an endpoint that signals a conflict with `return Response({'detail': ...}, status=409)` never appears in the logs — and neither do Django's own 404s. Which fix addresses the class of problem rather than this instance?
choices: Replace the manual return with a raised APIException subclass carrying status_code = 409, so the conflict travels the same path validation errors do and the existing handler logs it unchanged

Log from the last entry in MIDDLEWARE instead: middleware wraps every response on its way out, whatever produced it, so coverage stops depending on whether a view raised or returned — reading the body through getattr(response, 'data', None) since plain HttpResponse has no .data
Lower the django.request logger from CRITICAL to INFO so Django's built-in request logging reports the 409 and the 404 alongside the handler's richer lines
Override finalize_response on a shared base viewset, logging any response whose status_code is 400 or above before returning it — inside DRF, so .data is always present and correctly rendered
explanation: The bug is not a missing log line, it is a mechanism whose trigger is narrower than the concern: EXCEPTION_HANDLER fires only when a DRF exception is raised, so every error expressed as a returned Response — plus everything originating outside the view layer, like Django's 404s — is structurally invisible to it. Error logging is a cross-cutting concern over responses, and middleware is the layer whose contract matches: it sits outside the view stack and sees each finalized response regardless of origin, so placing it last in MIDDLEWARE (closest to the client on the way out) makes coverage a property of the stack rather than of each author's choices. Its one wrinkle is heterogeneous response types, which getattr(response, 'data', None) handles because DRF Response carries a parsed .data while HttpResponse offers only raw .content. Raising an APIException does light up this one endpoint, but it fixes an instance: it makes observability contingent on everyone remembering to raise rather than return, and forces exception-flavored control flow onto a perfectly ordinary conditional result — the next hand-returned 409 regresses silently, and Django-level errors remain unseen. Turning django.request back up buys a sparse built-in line without the body, and duplicates whatever your own handler already logs — the reason the standard setup silences django.request and namespaces a logger like api.request instead. Overriding finalize_response is the closest near-miss: it does catch returned responses, but only for views inheriting that base, so it scatters the concern across a class hierarchy and reintroduces the same gap the moment a viewset forgets the mixin or a non-DRF view answers.
